opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot.

The hardest part is that the field moves incredibly fast. When I started on XGBoost, and later TVM, the landscape looked very different. Now the models, the hardware, and the way people build and deploy AI systems change almost every year. So the challenge isn't just doing one good project. It's staying relevant and keeping your work useful when the ground keeps shifting.

For me, the answer has been to focus on the fundamental problems underneath the trends. The specific model architecture of the moment may change, but some questions keep coming back. How do we make machine learning run efficiently everywhere? How do we bridge the gap between new algorithms and very diverse hardware? How do we make these systems accessible, so it's not only a few big companies who can build and run them? If I anchor on those questions, I can adapt the methods without losing direction.

The second challenge is sustaining the open-source community. Building a tool is one thing. Keeping it alive for five or ten years is a very different problem. You need contributors who care, you need a healthy culture, and at some point the project has to grow beyond any single person, including me. That's not a technical problem, it's a people problem, and in some ways it's harder.

The third is personal: balancing depth and breadth. As a professor, and also working with startups and industry, there are many exciting things to do, and it's easy to spread yourself too thin. I try to remind myself to protect time for deep thinking and for working closely with students, because that's where the really new ideas come from.

So I'd say the challenge is to keep learning and keep a beginner's mindset, while still having the long-term patience to build things that last.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot. I'd say the hardest part is that the ground keeps moving under you. When we started things like XGBoost or TVM, the problems felt fairly well-defined: make gradient boosting fast and scalable, or build a compiler that can take a model and run it well on different hardware. But the field changes so quickly now. Every year there's a new model architecture, a new accelerator, a new serving pattern, and the abstractions you built two years ago may not fit anymore.

So the challenge isn't really writing more code. It's picking the right layer to build on so that the work stays relevant as everything above and below it shifts. For me the bet has been on machine learning systems and compilation, because no matter what the models look like, somebody still has to map them efficiently onto hardware. But you have to keep revisiting that bet.

The second part is community. Open source projects live or die on whether people keep contributing after the initial excitement fades. Sustaining that over a decade means mentoring new maintainers, being okay with the project evolving in directions you didn't plan, and sometimes stepping back so others can own pieces of it. That's as much a people problem as a technical one, and I think it's actually harder.

And then there's the personal side, balancing research, teaching, building products, and still having the time to actually sit down and think deeply about a problem. I don't think I've fully solved that one. But I try to focus on work where the research and the practical systems reinforce each other, so that I'm not splitting myself across things that pull in opposite directions.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest challenge is sustaining a clear sense of direction while staying open to change. In a field that moves quickly, there are always new problems that seem urgent. But some of the work that matters most takes years of patient effort, and you need to give it that time.

For me, that also means building a community where people can take ownership and bring their own ideas. You can only do so much yourself. Over the next five to ten years, the challenge is to keep learning and contributing while helping others carry the work forward in directions I might not have imagined.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest challenge is sustaining the ability to work on important, long-term problems while also responding to what people need today. With open-source work, there are always immediate things to improve, and those are valuable. But you also need space to step back and ask whether there’s a fundamentally better way to do things.

Over five or ten years, that also becomes a question about people. How do you build a community where others can take ownership, bring new ideas, and keep the work moving? I think the challenge is to keep learning myself while creating an environment where the work can grow beyond what I can do personally.
